abstract: Despite the widespread use of platinum drugs in cancer therapy, defining their mechanisms of action and predicting clinical outcomes remain challenging. Unlike cisplatin, which kills cells mainly through the DNA damage response, oxaliplatin toxicity is driven largely by nucleolar stress, yet how cells cope with this stress remains poorly understood. A nucleotide excision repair protein, damage-specific DNA binding protein 2 (DDB2), protects cells from oxaliplatin but not cisplatin, suggesting that it may preferentially engage oxaliplatin adducts. Using single-molecule analysis of DNA-binding proteins from nuclear extracts, we show that DDB2 binds both oxaliplatin and cisplatin intrastrand adducts. Oxaliplatin, but not cisplatin, drives progressive accumulation of DDB2 in nucleoli, pointing to a role at sites of oxaliplatin-induced nucleolar stress. The repair-deficient xeroderma pigmentosum group E K244E variant localizes to nucleoli but fails to rescue oxaliplatin sensitivity of DDB2-knockout cells, indicating that repair activity, not nucleolar localization alone, is required for protection. In colorectal cancer (CRC), elevated DDB2 levels correlate with higher oxaliplatin IC50, are higher in tumors than adjacent normal tissue by immunohistochemistry, and DDB2 transcript associates with non-response and shorter progression-free survival in FOLFOX-treated patients. Pharmacological inactivation or degradation of DDB2 synergizes with oxaliplatin, offering a biomarker-driven strategy to overcome chemoresistance.
